Modern.tagline: A modern wellness brand for the quiet hour.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Stillness is the archaic word for quiet motionlessness — single trade word with a meditation register. Wellness is the plain category suffix.
Modern.industrySummary: Wellness is one of the loudest categories that exists. Most brands are trying to sound calming while also yelling at you about your morning routine. There's an opening for a brand that lowers the volume in its own marketing.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Headspace (headspace.com) made meditation feel modern. Calm (calm.com) holds the consumer mindset space. Insight Timer (insighttimer.com) goes deeper for practitioners. Othership (othership.us) does the in-person version well. We sit closest to Othership in tone, in a different format.
Modern.positioningStatement: A wellness brand for people who want less wellness in their life, not more.
Modern.positioningRationale: Customers are over-served on wellness content, apps, products, supplements, and rituals. We are positioned against the entire add-more model. Subtraction is the offer.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 50. Tried three wellness apps and uninstalled all of them. Owns supplements they don't take. Wants their wellness to be quiet, low-friction, and not on their phone.

dos: Use short sentences
Tell customers when they don't need our product
Skip the inspirational quote

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. Stillness Wellness set in a soft modern grotesk, slightly humanist, with rounded terminals. A small breath-mark dot above the I of QUIET works as the app icon, used alone on profile photos and notification badges.

colorPalette.meaning: Overcast. Neutral. The opposite of bright.

colorPalette.meaning: Deep green. The single anchor color.

typography.primary: ABC Diatype Mono for the wordmark
typography.secondary: ABC Diatype for body and UI
typography.rationale: Disciplined, calm letterforms. Mono for the brand surface, regular for everything else. One family, two weights.

customSections.title: What it doesn't say
customSections.body: No mindfulness scripts. No 'morning routine' content. No founder yoga photos. No supplement upsells. No streak counters.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: An app that does one thing per session. Email once a month, three sentences long. A physical journal for sale that's actually beautiful. No push notifications, ever.

Modern.brandNameRationale: Lichen is a real plant — slow-growing, considered, slightly archaic in the wellness lexicon. Salt is the elemental opposite — mineral, plain, ancient. The pairing reads as botanical-plus-elemental, in the lineage of considered wellness brand names (The Nue Co, Apothékary, Saie) without imitating any of them. Avoids the standard 'Glow / Bloom / Aura' wellness vocabulary entirely.
Modern.manifesto: Modern wellness has become a vocabulary of vague positivity. Glow, bloom, balance, alignment. We made Lichen & Salt because the actual product is a small set of botanical and mineral remedies that have been used for hundreds of years. The brand is honest about that. No vague benefits, no 'unlock', no journey. A short catalog of working remedies, written plainly.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern wellness has split between the supplement-led DTC cohort (Care/of, Athletic Greens) and the apothecary-led brand cohort (The Nue Co, Apothékary). The opening is for a brand that takes the apothecary tradition further into plain language and short catalog discipline.
Modern.competitorLandscape: The Nue Co (thenueco.com) holds the considered apothecary slot. Apothékary (apothekary.com) plays in the botanical-modern peer position. Moon Juice (moonjuice.com) sits in the cult-wellness middle. We sit alongside The Nue Co with a quieter visual register and a more limited catalog.
Modern.positioningStatement: Lichen & Salt is a small modern apothecary brand offering a curated catalog of botanical and mineral remedies described plainly.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on catalog discipline and plain language. Fourteen products, each named for its primary ingredient, each described in one paragraph that names what it does and what it does not do.

targetAudience.primary: Adults 30–50 who have used supplements and are skeptical of the vocabulary.
motivations: Want plain language about what a product does.

dos: Name products by primary ingredient.
Write product copy in one paragraph.
State what the product does not do.
Sign emails with the formulator's first name.

messagingPillars.name: Fourteen products
messagingPillars.description: The catalog is fourteen items. We add slowly. Each product has a clear apothecary tradition behind it.

messagingPillars.name: Plain paragraphs
messagingPillars.description: Each product page is a single paragraph. We say what the product is made of, what it does, and what it does not do.

messagingPillars.name: Apothecary tradition
messagingPillars.description: Formulations are based on documented traditional use. We reference the historical practice on the back label.

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Lichen & Salt set in a quiet modern serif with a long ampersand. A small botanical illustration of a lichen branch sits above the wordmark on the bottle.

colorPalette.meaning: Primary — the color of weathered stone.

typography.primary: A quiet modern serif for the wordmark and product names.
typography.secondary: A neutral grotesque for body and ingredient lists.
typography.rationale: The serif sets the apothecary tone. The grotesque handles the working type.

Modern.mission: We compete on catalog discipline and plain language. Fourteen products, each named for its primary ingredient, each described in one paragraph that names what it does and what it does not do.
Modern.vision: A short catalog of working remedies, written plainly.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: The brand names what it provides, literally. A quiet room. The definite article makes it the one. The phrase reads as a service, a destination, and a state of mind in one go. No metaphor, no positioning trick. Just the room.
Luxury.story: The Quiet Room began with a single space in a Tribeca basement. Soundproofed walls, no phones, no clocks, one staff member to greet you and one timer to mark forty-five minutes. We thought a few other people would want it too. We were right.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury wellness has been trending toward bigger destinations, longer programs, and more measurable outcomes. There's a parallel market for something smaller, more old-world, more like a private library. People who pay for the absence of stimulation, not its presence.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Aman (aman.com) is the destination peer. Six Senses (sixsenses.com) carries the wellness-led hotel category. Equinox Hotels (equinoxhotels.com) leans wellness with branding. None of them offer this format: a small, urban, daily-use room. We are closer to a private members' club than a hotel.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A private room for people who need forty-five minutes away from everything.

targetAudience.primary: 35 to 65. Successful, time-poor, over-stimulated. Has tried the meditation apps. Has done the retreats. Wants something they can use in the middle of a Tuesday.

dos: Use few words
Address members by name in writing
Send a paper card on every renewal

Luxury.logoDirection: A wordmark in a classical serif. The Quiet Room set with wide kerning, in a single weight. A small horizontal line beneath the words, the threshold of the room itself. The mark is small, only appearing on the front door, the appointment card, and the receipt.

typography.rationale: A high contrast serif sets the tone. A modern grotesk handles the website and member portal. Both restrained.

customSections.body: No social media. No photography of the room. No press tours. No mentions of the wellness category. No content marketing.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Maison is the French commercial-house convention used by heritage perfume and apothecary brands (Maison Margiela, Maison Francis Kurkdjian). Aubray is a plausible French surname pulled from the registry of older apothecary houses — readable, slightly aristocratic, not famous. The pair places the brand in the heritage French apothecary tradition without imitating any existing maison.
Luxury.story: Maison Aubray is a French apothecary founded in 1894 and run by the founder's great-grandchildren. The catalog includes seventeen products, all formulated in the original Paris atelier. Products are sold through a small list of pharmacies and the maison's two boutiques.
Luxury.industrySummary: Heritage apothecary brands are rare and remain among the most premium wellness presentations available. There is space in the global market for a new entrant in the deeply traditional French apothecary register — multi-generational, atelier-based, small catalog.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Officine Universelle Buly (buly1803.com) is the closest reference in heritage register and atelier presentation. Santa Maria Novella (smnovella.com) holds the multi-century apothecary slot. Officine Panerai-style heritage maisons play in the broader category. We belong in the small French heritage apothecary tradition.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Maison Aubray is a French heritage apothecary in continuous family operation since 1894, offering seventeen products formulated in the original atelier.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not extend the catalog. The atelier is the limit. The seventeen products have remained the same for four generations, with formulation changes only when traditional ingredients have become unavailable.

targetAudience.primary: Buyers 35–65 with a long-term relationship with heritage personal-care brands.
behaviors: Re-buy the same products across years.
Travel to the maison when in Paris.
motivations: Want a brand with continuity of formula and family.
Want a small catalog they can know completely.

dos: Address customers in formal French and English.
Reference the maison's founding year.
Sign correspondence in the founders' family name.
Print all marketing communications.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word, two readings. The verb (to make quiet, to stop moving). The adjective (calm, unmoving). The brand is the state we are trying to reach.
Minimal.industrySummary: Wellness is overloaded with tools, apps, supplements, and protocols. There's a quiet market for a brand that strips everything back to the simplest practice. Breathing. That's it.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most apps in the category bundle breathing with meditation, journaling, mood tracking, and habit streaks. We don't. There isn't a direct competitor that does only this.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A breathing practice app. No meditation. No journaling. No mood tracker.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who already have a wellness practice and want one tool that does one thing. They distrust apps that try to do everything.

dos: Use the smallest number of words
Show the timer, the pattern, the breath count
Recommend offline practice often

Minimal.tagline: A small dose. A small word.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Mote is a real word for a tiny particle or speck. Archaic in everyday use, evocative, single-syllable. Stands in the lineage of one-word evocative wellness brand names (Lyma, Wisp, Tend) without being literal about wellness or health. Slightly poetic without being aspirational.
Minimal.manifesto: Wellness brands have grown into long product lines, complicated systems, and twelve-step rituals. We made Mote because the actual best practice is small — a single drop, a single capsule, a single five-minute exercise. The catalog is six products. The packaging is small. The instructions are one sentence.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal wellness has been claimed by the supplement subscription category but is under-represented in topical and ritual products. There is real space for a brand that takes the minimal premise into apothecary topicals, small-dose oils, and single-step rituals.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Tend (hellotend.com) plays in the minimal-modern wellness space. Wisp (hellowisp.com) holds the single-purpose minimal slot. Aesop (aesop.com) is the apothecary-minimal reference. We sit further out — fewer products, less language, smaller bottles.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Mote is a six-product apothecary brand of small-dose botanical oils and tinctures.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the catalog and the bottle. Six products, named for their use. Each bottle is small. Each instruction is one sentence.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Pillar suggests support, structure, and something a company is built on. Workplace Wellness names the buyer category cleanly. The whole name reads like a real, established B2B service firm.
Corporate.industrySummary: Employee wellness has matured from a perk into a measurable HR program. Companies have budget. Buyers want a single vendor who can stand up the program, run it, and report on outcomes. Most vendors lean app-only or consultancy-only. The opening is a structured operator.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Lyra Health (lyrahealth.com) is the mental health leader. Headspace for Work (headspace.com/work) carries the meditation B2B angle. Modern Health (joinmodernhealth.com) sits in the middle. Wellable (wellable.co) is the operations-led peer. We sit closest to Wellable, with stronger brand work.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Full-service workplace wellness, run by people who understand both HR and behavior change.
Corporate.positioningRationale: HR teams don't need another app to recommend. They need a partner who shows up, runs the program, files the reports, and renews the contract because the employees actually engaged.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Aldercroft is a compound English place-name — Alder (a tree) and croft (a small enclosed field). Reads as a real but unfamiliar regional location, which is the convention for established holding companies that take their names from where they were founded. Wellness Group signals the multi-brand operating structure. The pair sits firmly in the institutional holding-company register.
Corporate.manifesto: Aldercroft Wellness Group owns and operates a portfolio of wellness brands across supplements, topicals, and wellness services. Each brand retains its identity and formulation house; we operate the shared manufacturing, regulatory, distribution, and back-office infrastructure. The buyer is a wellness brand founder considering sale, a retail buyer seeking single-vendor supply, or an institutional investor holding wellness assets.
Corporate.industrySummary: Wellness has consolidated into a small number of large multi-brand operators (Unilever Prestige, Procter & Gamble Beauty, P&G Health). The opening is for a regional multi-brand wellness operator with manufacturing depth, regulatory infrastructure, and the procurement reliability major retailers require.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Unilever Prestige (unileverprestige.com) is the large peer at scale. Pharmavite (pharmavite.com) holds the supplement multi-brand slot. Nestlé Health Science (nestlehealthscience.com) sits in the health-and-wellness middle. We sit in the regional mid-tier multi-brand wellness operator category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Aldercroft Wellness Group is a regional multi-brand wellness operator running supplements, topicals, and wellness services under shared manufacturing, regulatory, and distribution infrastructure.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on manufacturing capacity, regulatory depth, and retailer-grade reliability. The brands keep their voice; the operations live with us.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Slow is the word that wellness optimization culture forgot. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school. Stands in the lineage of declarative-position creative wellness brands (Soft Animal Wellness).
Creative.manifesto: Most wellness brands sound like a yoga teacher who has just read three books. We sound like the friend you call when you need a break and a laugh. The brand is fun. The practice is real. The customer gets both.
Creative.industrySummary: Wellness branding has been quiet, ethereal, beige, and slightly precious for the last five years. There's room for one that's loud, warm, full of personality, and still serious about helping people slow down.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Calm and Headspace dominate the quiet-app space. Othership (othership.us) has the right tone in a different format. Liquid IV (liquid-iv.com) does playful wellness in beverage. We sit somewhere between Othership's tone and a totebag brand.
Creative.positioningStatement: Wellness products and content for people who want to take a break without becoming a different person.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 40. Has a busy job. Has tried two wellness apps. Wants a brand that doesn't lecture. Buys the totebag. Reads the newsletter. Doesn't post about it.

donts: Photograph people meditating in white linen

Creative.tagline: A wellness brand from a Mary Oliver line.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Soft Animal is taken from the Mary Oliver poem 'Wild Geese' — 'You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves.' The name is unusual, literary, warm, and instantly evocative of body-as-friend rather than body-as-project. The reference is recognizable to the brand's audience without being a quotation. Reads in the lineage of literary-creative wellness brands (Goop, Moon Juice, The Nue Co) without imitating any of them.
Creative.manifesto: Wellness marketing treats the body as a problem to be optimized. We started Soft Animal because the body is mostly fine and mostly knows what it wants — sleep, food, sun, water, the right amount of movement, the right amount of rest. The brand is a small set of products built around treating the body as a friend, not as a project to be perfected.
Creative.industrySummary: Wellness has been dominated by optimization vocabulary — biohacking, peak performance, longevity. There is real space for a creative-led brand built on the opposite stance — body as friend, smallness as the goal, softness as the value.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Goop (goop.com) plays in the cult-wellness slot. Moon Juice (moonjuice.com) holds the literary-creative peer position. The Nue Co (thenueco.com) sits in the considered-creative middle. Saie (saie.com) plays in the soft-modern peer space. We sit alongside Moon Juice with a more literary, less mystical register.
Creative.positioningStatement: Soft Animal Wellness is a creative wellness brand built around treating the body as a friend — a small catalog of products, a literary voice, no optimization language.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on tone. The catalog, photography, and voice all hold a single point of view — body as friend, not project.

targetAudience.primary: Adults 28–50 who are skeptical of wellness optimization and want a brand that argues for ease.
behaviors: Buy fewer products than they used to.
motivations: Want a wellness brand that is kind to the body.
Want to be talked to like a friend, not a project.
Want a brand with a clear point of view.

dos: Write product copy in the second person, warmly.
Reference the body as a friend.
Quote poems and essays in marketing.
Send a short literary note with every order.

messagingPillars.name: Small catalog
messagingPillars.description: Ten products, each tied to a specific small ritual — sleep, bath, morning, evening, rest, meal. We do not extend.

messagingPillars.name: Literary voice
messagingPillars.description: Marketing leans on quoted lines from poets and essayists who write kindly about the body. Each product is named with a literary fragment.

messagingPillars.name: A note with every order
messagingPillars.description: Every order ships with a short printed note — a poem, an essay fragment, a recipe. The note is the brand.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Soft Animal Wellness set in a quiet display serif, with a small hand-drawn illustration of a sleeping fox or rabbit beside it. The mark feels printed in a chapbook.

colorPalette.name: Rose
colorPalette.meaning: Single accent — the color of skin in warm light.

typography.primary: A quiet display serif for the wordmark and product names.
typography.secondary: A book serif for marketing copy and printed notes.
typography.rationale: The brand reads like a slim poetry chapbook. Both faces are quiet.

Creative.brandDescription: Soft Animal Wellness is a creative wellness brand built around treating the body as a friend — a small catalog of products, a literary voice, no optimization language.
Creative.mission: The brand competes on tone. The catalog, photography, and voice all hold a single point of view — body as friend, not project.
Creative.vision: The brand is a small set of products built around treating the body as a friend, not as a project to be perfected.
coreValues: Literary — we write more than we shout.
Warm — we are friendly, not formal.
Considered — we choose fewer things, more carefully.
Specific — generalities are how people avoid commitment.
Creative.scope:
Soft Animal Wellness works across:
• Small catalog
• Literary voice
• A note with every order
